sections.title: A deck, not a single card
paragraphs: One brilliant demo {{prompt}} proves nothing about day-two reliability. Production teams keep a deck of {{testCase}} cards: fixed questions they rerun after every change.
A {{testCase}} is more than wording: it names the task, includes realistic inputs and often tags the failure mode you fear (hallucination, rude tone, wrong format).
Together those cards form a {{goldenSet}}: the baseline suite you trust. When a {{model}} or {{prompt}} update lands, you redeal the same deck and check scores.
AiEval shines here: one {{evaluation}} can hold many prompts, shared {{rubric}} and multiple {{model}}s. Your golden deck lives in one place.
Next: what makes individual test cases worth keeping.
bullets: Tag failure modes you need to catch every release.

check.prompt: A PM says: "We tested the new {{model}} on one clever {{prompt}} in Slack. Ship it." What is missing?
check.answer: A golden set covering realistic failure modes
choices: Nothing: one great demo is enough
A golden set covering realistic failure modes
check.explanation: Single demos miss edge cases. A {{goldenSet}} of {{testCase}}s catches regressions that flashy one-offs never probe.

sections.title: What makes a strong test case
paragraphs: Strong {{testCase}}s are specific enough to score: clear output format, realistic domain detail and an expected quality bar (even if qualitative).
Include traps your users actually hit: ambiguous instructions, missing context, requests that should trigger refusal. Weak suites only contain easy wins.
Click each example to see whether it belongs in a {{goldenSet}}. "Interesting" is not the same as "diagnostic."
Balance breadth and maintenance: start with ten high-signal cases before chasing hundreds. Expand when production logs show new failure clusters.

reveals.prompt: Test case: "Write something nice about our product."
reveals.reveal: Too vague: no format, no facts to verify, hard to score consistently.

reveals.prompt: Test case: "Summarize this refund policy in three bullets; if policy is silent on EU returns, say 'not covered'."
reveals.reveal: Strong: concrete format plus an explicit edge-case behavior to check.
Risky: misses refusal, hallucination and hostile-input failures.

aside.title: Try in AiEval
aside.body: Create an {{evaluation}} with three to five fixed {{prompt}}s before you add a second {{model}}.

check.prompt: You are building a support-bot {{goldenSet}}. Which {{testCase}} is most diagnostic?
check.answer: User asks for a refund outside policy with angry tone
choices: User asks for a refund outside policy with angry tone
User asks the bot to write a poem
check.explanation: Policy edge cases plus tone stress refusal, accuracy and politeness: the failures that hurt real users.

sections.title: Test cases meet rubrics
paragraphs: {{testCase}}s define what you ask; {{rubric}} rows define how you score answers. You need both: prompts without criteria produce arguments, not measurements.
When a {{testCase}} fails, the {{criterion}} row tells you why: format break, missing fact, unsafe content. That pairing makes fixes actionable.
Next up: Rubrics and criteria, where you turn "better" into scorable rows with anchors every {{judge}} can apply.
bullets: Expand the deck when production logs show new failures.

check.prompt: In one short phrase: what is a {{goldenSet}}?
check.explanation: A {{goldenSet}} is the curated {{testCase}} deck you rerun to detect quality drops: the backbone of {{regressionEval}}.

recapQuestions.prompt: Why keep angry or edge-case prompts in a {{goldenSet}}?
recapQuestions.explanation: Happy-path-only suites green-light releases that fail on the prompts users actually send.

recapQuestions.prompt: A {{testCase}} passes but uses vague wording. What happens when you automate scoring?
recapQuestions.answer: Judges disagree on what better means
recapQuestions.explanation: Vague {{testCase}}s fight clear {{criterion}} anchors. Tighten prompts before scaling {{judge}} automation.
